title: Pierre Point: The Last Hangman
full_review:
The well-made British film, "Pierrepoint: The Last Hangman" (IFC), argues against capital punishment by telling the story of one of England's most prolific executioners. Between 1934 and 1955, Albert I. Pierrepoint (Timothy Spall) had a hand in the deaths of hundreds of condemned prisoners.

Staunch performances by two talented character actors -- Spall and Juliet Stevenson, who plays Pierrepoint's wife, Anne -- anchor the picture. Director Adrian Shergold, a protege of director Mike Leigh (whose stylistic influence is apparent), tackles a sensitive subject through the prism of one seemingly ordinary Briton.

While sympathetic to its real-life protagonist, there's no doubt this film takes a critical view of the death penalty, though the good intent is marred by some heavy-handedness. The topic is inherently visceral and Shergold frequently shifts angles, as if searching for a perspective that's neither understated nor histrionic. Wisely, he always returns to Spall's face, the physical embodiment of the moral tensions.

According to the portrait that emerges, Pierrepoint was not a monster but a meticulous civil servant who took pride in his grim work. His father and uncle had also been on the List of Executioners. A fastidious attention to detail and determination to be efficient insulated him from any qualms; ironically, this approach also meant he carried out his duties in a relatively humane manner. As expected, his attitude evolves over the course of the picture.

"Pierrepoint" is most successful at linking his story to the stereotypical mid-century British ethos. It's suggested that a stiff-upper-lip, dutiful mind-set -- both on a personal and societal level -- was a big reason capital punishment continued. Pierrepoint feels increasingly exploited by the government, especially after gaining notoriety for hanging scores of Nazi war criminals in Germany.

His disillusionment becomes acute during a devastatingly personal and hard-to-believe plot turn. While fact-based, this narrative hiccup raises more questions than it answers. The filmmakers don't intend to debate the issue on an intellectual level or reference any external moral authority, however. The goal is to have the audience identify with Pierrepoint and turn against the practice as his revulsion grows.

Aside from this one crucial event, "Pierrepoint" doesn't shock or sensationalize.

The film contains numerous nongraphic hangings, a mostly clothed adulterous encounter, full-frontal female and rear male nudity involving corpses, and a few instances of crass language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
